tables.title: Most common winning margins, 2016–2025
tables.note: 2639 games. Half a point matters most at 3, then 7, 6 and 10: that is how often the game lands exactly there.
tables.verdict: 14.4% of games are decided by exactly 3 and 8.5% by 7. Half a point is worth the most around those two numbers.

tables.title: Push rate when the spread sits on a key number
tables.note: How often the favorite won by exactly the spread.
tables.verdict: A spread of exactly 3 pushes 10.1% of the time; a spread of 7, 5.5%.

tables.title: Most common final totals
tables.note: Totals cluster far less than margins. No number comes close to 3 or 7.
tables.verdict: Totals do not cluster. The most common final total, 51, is 4.0% of games.

tables.title: Six-point teaser legs by spread, 2016–2025
tables.note: A leg is one side moved six points in your favor. A two-team teaser at 1.83 (−120) needs each leg to win about 73.9%; at 1.91 (−110), 72.4%. The textbook play is underdogs of 1–2.5 teased up through 3 and 7, and that one has cleared the bar. Favorites of 7.5–8.5 teased down have not.
tables.verdict: Underdogs of 1 to 2.5 teased up six win 76.2% of legs against a 73.9% bar. Favorites clear it only at a spread of exactly 7. Books that charge more than 1.83 for two teams erase the edge.

tables.title: Six-point teaser legs on totals
tables.note: Totals teasers have no key numbers working for them, and it shows.
tables.verdict: No total, teased either way, wins more than 70.3% of legs. The bar is 73.9%.

tables.title: Moneylines by spread size, 2016–2025
tables.note: Return per unit staked on every underdog, and on every favorite, to win outright at closing prices. A flat bettor loses the book's margin (about 4%) with no edge, so anything better than about −4% is beating the average.
tables.verdict: Underdogs of 10 or more return -21.9% and -15.1% on the moneyline. The smallest underdogs (1 to 2.5) lose the least, -1.3%.

tables.title: 2026 luck by team
tables.note: Sorted luckiest first. Expected wins come from points scored and allowed. Wins over expected, a lopsided one-score record, a big turnover margin and recovering well over half of all fumbles are the things that tend to drift back. Opponent FG = field goals opponents made against them.
tables.verdict: CLE has won 1.9 more games than its points say and TB 1.8 fewer. Both should drift back toward their point differential.

tables.title: Does luck reverse? Weeks 1–9 against the rest of the season, 2016–2025
tables.note: Teams are grouped by wins over expected through Week 9. A team's one-score record in the first half of a season has a correlation of +0.14 with its one-score record in the second half, which is to say none. Break-even against the spread is 52.4%.
rows: Luckiest fifth (won 1+ more than their points say)
tables.verdict: Lucky teams do fall back, from winning 72.2% of games to 55.7%, but they cover 48.7% afterwards. The spread sees it coming.

tables.title: Home-field advantage by season
tables.note: Average home margin was near three points a decade ago. The market's average home spread shows what it now prices in.
tables.verdict: Home teams won by 2.07 points a game in 2025 and the market priced 1.5. Home field is worth about two points now, not three.

tables.title: Home-field advantage by team, 2021–2026
tables.note: Home edge = half the gap between a team's average margin at home and on the road, which removes how good the team is. About 45 home games each, so the extremes are partly noise.
tables.verdict: The largest measured home edge is CHI at 4.9 points, on about 45 home games. Too few to adjust a line by.

tables.title: 2026 scoring by quarter, per game
tables.note: Sorted by first-half margin. Four games a team is a small sample; treat it as a description of the season so far.
tables.verdict: BAL has the best first-half margin (+9.3 a game) and TEN the worst (-8.9). Four games each.

tables.title: 2026 decisions and finishing
tables.note: Fourth-and-short = fourth down with 2 or fewer yards to go, outside the team's own 40, game still in the balance. League: goes for it 67% of the time; scores a touchdown on 63% of red-zone trips. Four games in, the fourth-down counts are tiny.
cols: TD on share of all drives
tables.verdict: The league goes for it on 67% of fourth-and-shorts and scores a touchdown on 63% of red-zone trips.

tables.title: Current head coaches against the spread, 2016–2026
tables.note: Coaches with at least eight games since 2016, all teams they have coached. Small samples swing wildly: a coach needs roughly 150 games before 55% means anything.
tables.verdict: Among coaches with 150+ games, the best is Sean Payton at 57.5% against the spread. Everyone above that on the list has a short track record.

tables.title: Each team's most recent starting quarterback, 2016–2026
tables.note: Career starts since 2016. Quarterbacks with 20+ starts are sorted by record against the spread; the rest follow.
tables.verdict: Among quarterbacks with 100+ starts, the best is Jared Goff at 57.2% against the spread. Shorter records above him are small samples.

tables.title: A quarterback's first three career starts (since 2017)
tables.note: Includes highly drafted rookies and emergency backups alike.
tables.verdict: A quarterback in his first three starts wins only 34.3% of the time but covers 50.0%. The spread already accounts for him.

tables.title: Referees working in 2026: results in their games, 2016–2026
tables.note: League average is 12.6 accepted penalties and 106 penalty yards a game. A referee works about 16 games a season, so even ten years is a small sample; sorted by share of overs. Upcoming assignments show when the league has posted them.
tables.verdict: Referees with 100+ games range from 42.4% to 52.0% overs, which is about what chance alone produces.

tables.title: Do flag-happy crews change totals?
tables.note: Referees grouped by their career penalties per game.
tables.verdict: Crews that throw the most flags: 48.8% overs. The fewest: 47.7%. Penalties do not move totals.

tables.title: Situational records
tables.note: Records are for the team in the spot. The ten-year column is the test; break-even is 52.4%. Nothing here is strong enough to bet blind.
rows: After a loss as a favorite
After a win as an underdog
Home after two straight on the road
West Coast team, early kickoff on the road
Second meeting with a division rival
Off a bye, on the road
tables.verdict: All 12 spots land between 48.1% and 52.7% against the spread over ten years. None is worth a bet by itself.

tables.title: Wind, outdoor games
tables.note: Wind is measured at kickoff, so this is not quite a pre-game number. Unders at 10–19 mph are the only weather effect here that has beaten the total; the 20+ row is 41 games.
tables.verdict: Unders hit 57.9% in outdoor games with 10 to 19 mph wind (525 games). Wind is the one weather effect the total has not fully absorbed.

tables.title: Time slot
tables.verdict: Sunday night and Monday night unders: 56.3% over 359 games. Every other slot is a coin flip.

tables.title: Playing surface, 2016–2025
tables.note: Turf games score more, and the total already knows it.
tables.verdict: Turf games score more (46.9 points against 44.6 on grass) and the total is already set higher.

tables.title: Temperature, outdoor games
tables.verdict: Freezing games score 41.3 points against a total of 43.0, but that is 88 games. The total already drops with the temperature.

tables.title: How often each role scores a touchdown, by the team's implied points, 2016–2025
tables.note: Role = rank on the team by touches per game so far that season (carries plus targets), from Week 3 on. Useful as a sanity check on the ATD tab: fair decimal odds are 1 divided by the rate.
tables.verdict: A lead back scores in 28.3% of games when his team is implied under 17.5 points and 56.7% at 27 or more. A top receiver: 21.6% and 41.0%.

tables.title: Reaching 100 yards, by season average coming in
tables.note: A back averaging 85–99 rushing yards reaches 100 well under half the time; a player's own average is closer to a coin flip than a floor. Matches own average = reaches the bottom of his bracket.
tables.verdict: A back averaging 85 to 99 rushing yards reaches 100 in 31.0% of games. A season average is nearer a coin flip than a floor.
